rv.q: Allen, taut and drawn, scopes this complexity deftly, though she doesn't quite plumb the depths of Katurian's own moral ambiguity.

If The Pillowman had trigger warnings – which, intriguingly, it doesn’t – they would be off the Richter scale. “Retard”, “spastic”, “Jew boy” – you name it, McDonagh includes it, in a smart, spiky but uneven and overlong script that builds layers of artifice and evil and has at its core an examination of the role and rights of the artist.
I think 'The Pillowman' could be more than this dark, funny, thrilling but ultimately contrived revival.
Matthew Dunster's production is too low voltage and deliberate to crackle.
There is a potentially explosive brilliance in this play, but its many ideas do not make a coherent whole here.
But this time around it left me indifferent and bored.

“Whoever wrote this,” snarls a policeman about Katurian’s prose, “is a sick, f***ing, scummy c***.” Ha ha ha, went perhaps five people in the audience. Never before, when seeing a character suffocated, have I felt such sharp envy.
Sharply funny, gasp-inducing and richly thought-provoking, this is a bold, uncompromising drama that startlingly interrogates its own artistic medium.
Dunster's impeccable directing means the audience can't help but remain gripped throughout.
At a time when safe revivals outnumber edgy new work in the West End, this must be, if you can forgive Allen's lite acting, the most disturbing play in town.

We have lived through two difficult decades since this play was first seen; perhaps its language and ideas aren't so shocking now, though still just as disturbing. It doesn't seem quite the winner 2003 thought it.

Martin McDonagh’s absurdist and sinister black comedy THE PILLOWMAN has begun a London revival at the Duke of York’s which is set to continue through the summer. The play was first presented at the National Theatre back in 2003, with David Tennant and Jim Broadbent.

“Martin McDonagh’s ‘The Pillowman’ is dark as ink, a fascinating defence of the power of the imagination and the freedom of the writer that shocks and unsettles with virtually every word...I’d never seen ‘The Pillowman’ before but had been assured by admirers of its quality.
Only a psychopath could endure more than five seconds of this inhumane bilge.

cn.t: McDonagh's dark, provocative play divides critics: some praise its sharp wit and bold interrogation of artistic freedom, while others dismiss it as shallow Grand Guignol. Allen's performance proves polarizing in this long-awaited West End bow.
